title: State
subtitle: Where a SwiftUI view keeps memory that survives its own recreation.

sections.body:
A SwiftUI view is a struct. It's created, its `body` is read, and it's thrown away — constantly, many times a second during an animation. So a plain `var` in a view is useless as memory: the next recreation resets it.

`@State` solves that by keeping the value *outside* the struct. SwiftUI allocates storage attached to the view's position in the hierarchy, and the property wrapper reads and writes that storage. The struct comes and goes; the state stays.

Writing to it also tells SwiftUI the view is invalid, so `body` is re-read and the UI updates. That's the whole loop: state changes, body re-runs, the framework diffs the result.

A view struct is a recipe, not a cake.

SwiftUI reads the recipe whenever it needs to know what the cake should look like, and the recipe itself is disposable — you can print a fresh copy any time.

`@State` is the pantry. It isn't part of the recipe, it's the ingredients kept in the kitchen, and it survives printing a new copy of the recipe. Which shelf your ingredients sit on is determined by where in the kitchen you are — that's view identity, and it's why moving a view can lose its state.

sections.caption: `@State` is owned by one view. `$` projects a Binding for children to write through.

sections.title: State survives view recreation
sections.altText: A view struct is created and discarded repeatedly, while its State storage persists outside, attached to the view's identity in the hierarchy.

steps.caption: The struct is created and its body read.
It's discarded and recreated — but the storage is untouched.
SwiftUI finds the right storage by view identity. Change the identity and you get fresh state.

sections.body:
`@State` is a property wrapper holding a *reference* to storage SwiftUI manages, keyed by the view's identity — its type and position in the hierarchy, or its `id` if you gave it one. That indirection is why a `let` view struct can still mutate `count`: the struct isn't changing, the box it points at is.

Identity is the part that produces surprises. Change a view's identity — with a different `.id()`, by moving it between branches of an `if`, or by changing an element's identity in a `ForEach` — and SwiftUI treats it as a new view and gives it *fresh* state. That's the mechanism behind both "my state mysteriously reset" and the deliberate trick of `.id(someValue)` to force a reset.

The initial value is only used the first time. On later recreations the existing storage wins, so passing a constructor argument into a `@State` initial value doesn't update it when the argument changes — a genuinely common bug.

`@State` is also the reason `body` must stay cheap: any write re-reads it.

sections.title: Initialising @State from a parameter
sections.body:
`@State private var name: String` initialised from an `init` parameter takes that value *once*. When the parent re-renders with a different value, the state keeps the old one, because storage already exists and the initial value is ignored.

If the parent owns the value, pass a `Binding` instead. If the child should reset when the input changes, give the child `.id(input)` so it gets a new identity, and with it fresh state.
View structs are disposable; `@State` is storage SwiftUI keeps alongside them, keyed by view identity. Own state where it belongs, keep it private, and remember that changing identity resets it.

title: Binding
subtitle: A read-write reference to state that lives somewhere else.

sections.body:
A `Binding` is a two-way connection to a value owned by another view. It doesn't store anything — it's a pair of closures, a getter and a setter, pointing at somebody else's storage.

That's what lets a child mutate a parent's state without owning it, and without the parent passing down a callback for every field. `TextField`, `Toggle` and `Slider` all take one, which is why they can write back the value you handed them.

You make one with the `$` prefix on a `@State` property. Data flows down as a value, changes flow back up through the setter.

A binding is a remote control, not a television.

Handing someone the remote lets them change the channel on your TV. They don't own the TV, they can't take it home, and there's still only one of it — but they can operate it from where they are.

Passing a plain value instead would be like handing them a photograph of the screen. They can look at it, and nothing they do affects what's actually on.

sections.caption: `@Binding` declares the dependency; `$` creates one to pass on.

sections.body:
`Binding` is a struct holding a `get` closure and a `set` closure. There's no storage in it at all, which is why passing one around is cheap and why a binding to a deallocated source is a real hazard rather than an impossible state.

The `$` prefix is the property wrapper's *projected value*: `@State` exposes `projectedValue` of type `Binding<Value>`, and `$count` is sugar for `_count.projectedValue`. Any property wrapper can project something; `@State`, `@Binding`, `@Bindable` and `@FocusState` all project bindings.

Because it's just closures, you can build one by hand with `Binding(get:set:)` — useful for deriving a transformed binding, bridging to a non-SwiftUI model, or adapting an optional. `.constant(_)` is the same thing with a setter that discards, which is what previews want.

sections.title: Passing a value where a binding was needed
sections.body:
`SettingRow(isOn: isOn)` compiles if the property is a plain `Bool`, and the row will display correctly — but the toggle's changes go nowhere and the parent never updates. It looks like a broken control rather than a data-flow mistake.

The rule is simple: if the child needs to *write*, it takes `@Binding` and you pass `$`. If it only displays, a plain `let` is better — it documents that the child can't change anything.
A binding is a getter/setter pair pointing at someone else's storage. Pass `$` when the child must write, and a plain value when it only reads.

title: Observation
subtitle: @Observable, and how SwiftUI learns which views depend on which properties.

sections.body:
`@Observable` is a macro that makes a reference type's properties trackable. A SwiftUI view that reads one of those properties in `body` is automatically re-rendered when *that property* changes — and not when others do.

That per-property precision is the whole improvement over `ObservableObject`. With `@Published`, any change fired `objectWillChange`, so every observing view re-rendered regardless of what it actually read. With Observation, a view reading only `name` doesn't care that `progress` changed.

It also removes the property-wrapper bookkeeping. No `@Published` on each property, and in a view you use plain `let`, or `@State` when the view owns the model's lifetime.

`ObservableObject` was a building fire alarm. Anything happens anywhere and everybody evacuates, whether or not it concerned them.

`@Observable` is a per-desk notification. You subscribed to the printer queue, so you hear about the printer — the fact that someone changed the thermostat doesn't reach you at all.

You didn't fill in a subscription form either. The system noticed what you looked at.

sections.caption: `@State` to own the model, plain `let` to pass it, `@Bindable` when you need `$`.

sections.title: Per-property dependency tracking
sections.altText: Two views read different properties of one Observable model. Changing one property re-renders only the view that read it.

steps.caption: Each view's body reads specific properties, and the framework records which.
Only the view that read `name` is invalidated. The other doesn't re-render.

sections.body:
The macro rewrites each stored property into a computed one that calls `access(keyPath:)` on read and `withMutation(keyPath:)` on write, backed by an `ObservationRegistrar`.

SwiftUI evaluates `body` inside `withObservationTracking`, so every property accessed during that evaluation is recorded as a dependency of that view. When one of those properties is mutated, the registrar notifies exactly the views that read it.

Two consequences worth internalising. First, tracking is per *access during body*, so a property read in a method you call from `body` is still tracked, while one read in a button's action closure is not — that closure isn't part of body evaluation. Second, reading a whole collection tracks the collection, so appending to an array re-renders everything that read it, no matter how granular the model looks.

It's also not SwiftUI-specific: `withObservationTracking` is in the Observation module and usable from plain Swift.

sections.title: Storing an @Observable model in @State in the wrong view
sections.body:
`@State private var model = Model()` creates the model once and ties its lifetime to *that view's identity*. Put it in a view that gets recreated with a new identity and the model is rebuilt, silently losing everything in it.

Own the model at the level whose lifetime should match it, and pass it down as a plain `let` or through the environment. Passing it down doesn't weaken tracking — that works regardless of how the reference arrived.

`@Observable` tracks reads at property granularity during body evaluation, so only views that actually read a property re-render when it changes. Own the model where its lifetime belongs, and pass it down plainly.
